Therefore, his audacity was chastised by Dorvillius in his <term>Vannus critica</term> <gloss>Critical Winnowing-basket/Sieve</gloss>, Amsterdam 1737, 8vo. This edition was published at Utrecht in 1732, 4to, for in the edition of the previous century, 1753, only the title page of the book was changed. But anyone who has the work of Fischer alone will easily dispense with these editions. He published the poems of Anacreon for the third time in Leipzig, 1793, 8vo, with the annotations of Baxter, Estienne, Faber, and his own, which are very rich in both critical and grammatical content, as well as a most comprehensive variety of readings. See the note on the reading of the Spaletti edition at number 21. Although the very learned old man repeated the poor revision of Baxter, he nevertheless performed a great service for Greek letters through this work of his. For he first added to this third edition the preface of the second edition, in which he discourses most diligently and with no small subtlety of mind on the value of various editions and on those matters which pertain to the literary study of these poems, and inquires whether these poems are rightly attributed to Anacreon. Furthermore, he increased the number of fragments and added epigrams of Greek poets on Anacreon. Compare the preface of Mehlhorn, page VI. The revision of Brunck is entirely new; using the Palatine manuscript <note>original: "Codex Palatinus"</note> copied by Spaletti, and the conjectures of Salmasius, Lennep, and others, he presented a more corrected Anacreon, but also indulging too much in his own wit, he emended many things in passing without providing any reasons. Now I devote my efforts to settling affairs, so that if our friend, that patron of the fine arts, reaches that highest pinnacle of dignity, we may hasten there as soon as possible. For he has often declared, most lovingly, both in letters and in direct conversation, that he wishes to look after my interests. For me, however, everything depends on being allowed to enjoy literary leisure, with no concern for domestic matters to interrupt. If we achieve this, let ambition thrive; we will live for ourselves and the Muses, and indeed with this spirit, that we attribute everything to God, on whom alone true happiness depends: that this seems the same to you, I easily infer from your letters. I am held by a wonderful desire to come to you: but many things snatch this opportunity away, especially my sick son, who I am firmly convinced is most dear to you, both for the sake of our friendship and for our new connection. If I hear that you have been strengthened after your illness, I will bear these domestic inconveniences with a calmer mind. Therefore, you will grant this to our love, which your virtue brought forth, your kindness nourishes, and increases, that you will also take the most diligent care of your health for our sake. # and the six blameworthy morals of the old

they also fail. Fearing therefore to suffer defect, they are illiberal. Again, they are illiberal because of the experience of time. Because, since they have lived for many years, it is credible that they have suffered many needs. Fearing therefore to suffer need, they are illiberal. It happens also that they are illiberal because they live more by memory than by hope. For they think of having lived much in the past and being about to live little in the future. And because memory is of past things and hope is of future things, therefore they do not live by hope, nor do they confide in those things which they ought to acquire in the future, but they live by memory, confiding in those things which they have acquired in the past. Therefore they are illiberal, not distributing easily what has been acquired. Fifth, they are of bad hope. For they hope for nothing good, but believe themselves to fail in everything. For hope is of future things, memory of past things. Since, therefore, the old have lived much in the past and believe themselves about to live little in the future, therefore they fail in hoping and think they will do little things. For they do not live and delight in hoping, but rather in remembering; therefore they are of difficult hope. Sixth, they are shameless and unblushing. For because the old are illiberal, they care more about the vile than about the honest. And thus they study more those things which import utility than those things which require the state of honor. Therefore, since modesty is the fear of dishonor, it does not apply to the old because they themselves care more about utility than about honor. Whence, the reason why someone is modest, as the philosopher says, is this: because he seeks to be had in honor and to be reputed honest. But the old, just as they fail in life and in humors and in natural heat, so they fail in spirit, not caring about how they are reputed; wherefore it happens that they are shameless. One cause could also be assigned, which is common to all things touched upon. For the old are cold. For it belongs to the cold to constipate and constrain; therefore, the old, from coldness, are constipated and retracted in themselves and rendered as if immobile, so that they dare nothing, believe nothing, hope for nothing, do not care to excel nor to be reputed. <note>A marginal mark resembles a hand or flourish.</note> Having elicited the morals of the young and the old, both praiseworthy and detestable, the morals of those who are in the [intermediate] state are easily patent. For they are in a state that mediates between the old and the young. Whatever of praiseworthiness is found in the young or in the old can be in those who are in the state. For they are not too hot as the young, nor too cold as the old; they hold the mean between both. Therefore, they are timid where one ought to fear, and bold where one ought to be bold. Similarly, because they are not inexperienced in everything as the young, nor deceived in everything as the old, therefore they do not believe everything as the young do because of inexperience, nor do they disbelieve entirely as the old do, in that the old are deceived in many things; but they behave in a middle way. Therefore, in the second [book] of the Rhetoric, it is said that those who are in the state are not believing everything nor disbelieving everything, but judge more according to truth. Furthermore, they are not impatient as the young, nor fearful and useless as the old. But as it is said in the second [book] of the Rhetoric, they are manly in temperance and tempered in manliness. Universally, I shall say that whatever of praiseworthiness is found in the old or in the young can be found in those who are in the state. And whatever of blameworthiness is found in the old or in the young can be excluded by those who are in the state. Thus, therefore, one must speak about the morals of men. Not, however, that these things have necessity, because the old can be liberal and magnanimous, and the young can also be tempered and stable. But these things are to be understood according to a certain propensity and inclination that is according to the natural course and order. Therefore, it follows that the master ought to be an orderer. Whence the master consists in equating. It is said that he who departs more from reality departs through an abundance of reason. *Meus, mea, meum*—of what mode of pronoun is it? The third. Why? Because it is declined through all its cases to the similarity of nouns of the first and second declension, that is, like *bonus, bona, bonum*, except for the vocative *mi*, from the vocative *mee*, where the double and short *e* has been changed into a long *i*, as *o mi pater, o mi fili* <gloss>o my father, o my son</gloss> instead of *mee pater, mee fili*.
